Where it began

Nuncargate, a small Nottinghamshire village close to Kirkby-in-Ashfield, is where Harold Larwood came into the world on 14 November 1904. His father, a miner, captained the village team. Harold left school at 13 and was soon working at Annesley Colliery, looking after the pit ponies. He bowled for Nuncargate's second team, in his first season taking 76 wickets, and by 1920 he was playing for the senior side with his dad, in plimsolls because proper boots were beyond the family budget.

Joe Hardstaff senior, the Nottinghamshire and England batsman, lived in the village and sent him for a trial at Trent Bridge in 1923. One senior player thought the slight teenager looked more like a jockey. By the end of the session he had a contract.

The player

His first Test came in 1926, when he had played just two seasons for the county, and that summer he helped win back the Ashes at The Oval. He topped the national averages in 1927 and became a Wisden Cricketer of the Year. On the 1928–29 tour of Australia he took 6 for 32 in the first Test at Brisbane, which stayed the best innings figures of his Test career.

His greatest series was in Australia in 1932–33, when captain Douglas Jardine built his whole plan around him. He was England's leading bowler with 33 wickets as the Ashes were won 4–1, and he made 98 as a nightwatchman in the final Test. In all he played 21 Tests from 1926 to 1933 and took 78 wickets at 28.36.

What made him special

Speed, above all, with accuracy to go with it. Jack Hobbs, who faced him many times, rated him the fastest and the most accurate bowler he ever saw. He was short for a fast bowler, but long arms and a smooth, almost silent run-up gave him a lovely side-on action that Neville Cardus thought entirely classical. The young Ray Lindwall watched him as a schoolboy and copied it.

He could bat a bit too: across all first-class cricket he made three hundreds to go with 1,427 wickets.

Away from the middle

After leaving the game he grew vegetables and ran a sweet shop in Blackpool. In 1949 the MCC made him an honorary member, and in 1950, encouraged by his old opponent Jack Fingleton, he moved his family to Australia, where he was welcomed warmly. He worked for a soft drinks firm in Sydney, with some writing and broadcasting on the side.

Trent Bridge opened the Larwood and Voce Stand in 1985, the Sydney Cricket Ground gave him life membership the same year, and in 1993 he was made an MBE. He died in 1995, aged 90.

And finally

In Sydney, Fingleton arranged for him to meet the former prime minister Ben Chifley. Between a broad Nottinghamshire accent and a broad Australian one, neither man could understand a word the other said, so Fingleton had to interpret. It was a fine start to a happy new life in a country whose batsmen had once wished him anywhere else.
